lessonTitle: Adrenergic Agonists and Antagonists: Alpha and Beta Receptor Pharmacology

blocks.text: A young woman stung by a wasp collapses with wheeze, swollen lips and a falling blood pressure. An intramuscular injection of adrenaline reverses all three problems within minutes: the airways open, the vessels tighten and the heart pumps harder. One drug, three opposite-looking tasks, because it acts on three different receptor subtypes.

blocks.markdown: The sympathetic nervous system acts through **noradrenaline** (released from nerve terminals) and **adrenaline** (released from the adrenal medulla) on **adrenoceptors**. All are G-protein-coupled receptors. Their subtypes are distributed differently in different tissues, so the effect of a drug depends on which subtype it hits. The key is to link each **subtype** to its **tissue** and its **effect**.

blocks.title: Adrenoceptor subtype and selectivity
blocks.text: Adrenoceptors are divided into alpha-1, alpha-2, beta-1, beta-2 and beta-3. Alpha-1 acts through Gq, alpha-2 through Gi, and all beta receptors through Gs. A drug is described as selective if at therapeutic doses it acts mainly on one subtype (for example bisoprolol on beta-1) and non-selective if it acts on several (for example propranolol on beta-1 and beta-2). Selectivity is dose-dependent and relative, not absolute.

blocks.caption: Adrenoceptor subtypes, principal effects and example drugs.
rows: Vasoconstriction (raised blood pressure), pupil dilation (mydriasis), bladder neck and prostate contraction
Presynaptic inhibition of noradrenaline release (central: lowers sympathetic outflow and blood pressure)
Heart: increased rate and force of contraction; kidney: renin release
Bronchodilation, vasodilation in skeletal muscle, uterine relaxation, tremor, hypokalaemia

blocks.title: Predicting the effect of an adrenergic agonist
blocks.prompt: Predict the effect on blood pressure and heart rate when (a) noradrenaline is infused (mainly alpha-1 and beta-1) and (b) isoprenaline is infused (beta-1 and beta-2, no alpha). Teaching example.

steps.text: Identify the receptors each drug activates. Noradrenaline: alpha-1 (strong), beta-1 (strong), beta-2 (weak). Isoprenaline: beta-1 and beta-2 only.
Noradrenaline: alpha-1 causes widespread vasoconstriction, raising systemic vascular resistance and blood pressure; beta-1 would raise heart rate directly.

Consider the reflex. The rise in pressure is sensed by baroreceptors, which increase vagal tone. This reflex bradycardia usually outweighs direct beta-1 stimulation, so heart rate often stays the same or falls.

Isoprenaline: beta-1 raises heart rate and contractility; beta-2 dilates skeletal-muscle arterioles, lowering diastolic pressure. Systolic pressure may rise slightly but mean pressure falls or is unchanged, and heart rate rises (with no vasoconstriction to trigger a reflex).

blocks.answer: Noradrenaline: blood pressure rises with a variable or reduced heart rate. Isoprenaline: heart rate rises, diastolic pressure falls and pulse pressure widens.

blocks.markdown: **How beta-blockers lower heart rate and blood pressure.** Beta-1 receptors in the sinoatrial node, atrioventricular node and myocardium are driven by Gs, adenylyl cyclase and cyclic AMP. A beta-blocker is a competitive antagonist at these receptors, so it blocks the effect of sympathetic stimulation. Heart rate and contractility fall, so cardiac output falls. Beta-1 receptors on the juxtaglomerular cells of the kidney also trigger renin release, so blocking them reduces angiotensin II and aldosterone. Together with some central effects, this lowers blood pressure over days to weeks.

blocks.latex: CO = HR \times SV, \qquad MAP \approx CO \times SVR
blocks.caption: CO = cardiac output (L/min); HR = heart rate (beats/min); SV = stroke volume (L/beat); MAP = mean arterial pressure; SVR = systemic vascular resistance.

blocks.title: Effect of a beta-blocker on cardiac output
blocks.prompt: A patient has a resting heart rate of 80 beats/min and a stroke volume of 70 mL. A beta-blocker lowers the heart rate to 60 beats/min with unchanged stroke volume. Calculate the cardiac output before and after, and the percentage fall.

steps.text: Convert stroke volume to litres: 70 mL = 0.070 L.
Percentage fall = (5.6 - 4.2) / 5.6 = 0.25, i.e. 25%. Because MAP is approximately CO times SVR, a fall in CO lowers blood pressure unless SVR rises to compensate.

blocks.answer: CO falls from 5.6 to 4.2 L/min, a 25% fall

blocks.title: Blood pressure lowering by beta-blockade
blocks.text: Beta-blockers lower heart rate and contractility (beta-1 in the heart) and reduce renin release (beta-1 in the kidney). Blocking beta-2 receptors adds no benefit for blood pressure and causes unwanted effects, which is why cardioselective agents are often preferred.

blocks.markdown: **Non-selective beta-blockers and asthma.** Beta-2 receptors in bronchial smooth muscle keep the airways dilated under sympathetic tone. A non-selective beta-blocker such as propranolol blocks them, so it can cause bronchoconstriction and may provoke severe, sometimes fatal, asthma attacks. In patients with asthma, non-selective beta-blockers are generally contraindicated. **Cardioselective** agents (beta-1 selective, such as bisoprolol or atenolol) are less likely to affect the airways but selectivity is lost at higher doses, so they are used only with great caution, with specialist advice and monitoring, and never in acute or unstable asthma.

items: Non-selective beta-blockers (propranolol, nadolol, sotalol, timolol) block beta-2: risk of bronchospasm.
Selective agents (bisoprolol, atenolol, metoprolol) are beta-1 preferring but not beta-1 specific.
Beta-blockers can blunt the warning symptoms of hypoglycaemia (tremor, palpitations) in people with diabetes treated with insulin or sulfonylureas.
Other cautions: heart block, severe bradycardia, peripheral vascular disease and acute heart failure.

blocks.title: Asthma and beta-blockers
blocks.text: Beta-blocker eye drops used for glaucoma (for example timolol) can be absorbed systemically and cause bronchospasm in asthma. Always ask about asthma before prescribing any beta-blocker, including topical ones.

blocks.title: Receptor to effect
blocks.text: Remember: beta-1 is in the heart (1 heart), beta-2 is in the lung (2 lungs). Alpha-1 constricts vessels, alpha-2 acts as the presynaptic brake, and beta-2 relaxes smooth muscle in bronchi and skeletal muscle vessels.

points: Alpha-1 causes vasoconstriction and mydriasis; alpha-2 inhibits noradrenaline release; beta-1 stimulates the heart and renin release; beta-2 relaxes bronchial and vascular smooth muscle.
Beta-blockers reduce heart rate, contractility and renin release, lowering cardiac output and blood pressure.
Non-selective beta-blockers block beta-2 receptors and can cause dangerous bronchoconstriction in asthma; cardioselective agents are safer but not risk-free.

questions.stem: Stimulation of which adrenoceptor subtype in the sinoatrial node increases heart rate?

options.text: Beta-1
Beta-2
Alpha-1
Alpha-2

distractorRationale.a: Correct: cardiac beta-1 receptors increase rate and contractility via Gs and cAMP.
distractorRationale.b: Incorrect: beta-2 receptors mainly relax smooth muscle in bronchi and vessels.
distractorRationale.d: Incorrect: alpha-2 is inhibitory and reduces transmitter release.

questions.explanation: Cardiac pacemaker and myocardial cells express mainly beta-1 receptors, which act through Gs to raise cAMP and increase heart rate and force. This is why beta-1 blockade slows the heart.

questions.stem: Phenylephrine eye drops are used to dilate the pupil for fundus examination. Which mechanism explains this?

options.text: Alpha-1 receptor stimulation contracts the radial muscle of the iris
Beta-2 receptor stimulation relaxes the sphincter pupillae
Alpha-2 receptor blockade increases aqueous humour production
Beta-1 receptor stimulation contracts the ciliary body

questions.correctOptionText: Alpha-1 receptor stimulation contracts the radial muscle of the iris

distractorRationale.a: Correct: phenylephrine is an alpha-1 agonist; the radial (dilator) muscle contracts, producing mydriasis.
distractorRationale.b: Incorrect: phenylephrine is not a beta-2 agonist and the sphincter is muscarinic-controlled.
distractorRationale.c: Incorrect: this does not describe mydriasis and phenylephrine is an agonist, not an alpha-2 blocker.
distractorRationale.d: Incorrect: ciliary contraction is muscarinic and relates to accommodation.

questions.explanation: Phenylephrine is a selective alpha-1 agonist. Alpha-1 stimulation of the iris radial muscle widens the pupil without affecting accommodation.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man with asthma uses salbutamol and notices a fine tremor of his hands and a mild tachycardia after several doses. Which receptor subtype best explains the tremor?

options.text: Beta-2 receptors in skeletal muscle
Alpha-1 receptors in skin vessels
Beta-1 receptors in the kidney
Alpha-2 receptors in the brainstem

distractorRationale.a: Correct: beta-2 stimulation of skeletal muscle causes tremor and is also linked to hypokalaemia.
distractorRationale.b: Incorrect: alpha-1 causes vasoconstriction, not tremor.
distractorRationale.c: Incorrect: renal beta-1 receptors release renin.
distractorRationale.d: Incorrect: alpha-2 stimulation in the brainstem reduces sympathetic outflow.

questions.explanation: Salbutamol is a beta-2 selective agonist. Beta-2 receptors in skeletal muscle cause tremor as a common unwanted effect, while some tachycardia arises from beta-2 effects on the heart and vessels and partial beta-1 action.

questions.stem: A patient has a resting heart rate of 90 beats/min and a stroke volume of 60 mL. After starting a beta-blocker the heart rate is 65 beats/min and the stroke volume is unchanged. Calculate the new cardiac output in L/min.
questions.explanation: Cardiac output = HR x SV = 65 x 0.060 L = 3.9 L/min. It was 5.4 L/min before treatment, so the beta-blocker has reduced output by about 28%, which contributes to the fall in blood pressure.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a recognised mechanism by which beta-blockers lower blood pressure?

options.text: Reduced renin release from the juxtaglomerular cells
Direct vasodilation through beta-2 stimulation
Increased venous return from alpha-1 blockade
Increased vagal output to the kidney

questions.correctOptionText: Reduced renin release from the juxtaglomerular cells

distractorRationale.a: Correct: renal beta-1 blockade lowers renin, angiotensin II and aldosterone.
distractorRationale.b: Incorrect: beta-blockers antagonise, not stimulate, beta-2 receptors.
distractorRationale.c: Incorrect: pure beta-blockers do not block alpha-1 receptors.
distractorRationale.d: Incorrect: this is not a mechanism of beta-blockade.

questions.explanation: Besides slowing the heart, beta-blockers block beta-1 receptors on juxtaglomerular cells, reducing renin secretion and so the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone drive on blood pressure. They do not act as vasodilators in the way alpha-blockers or calcium channel blockers do.

questions.stem: Explain, in terms of receptors and signalling, why a beta-1 selective blocker lowers heart rate and blood pressure.
markingGuide: Beta-1 receptors in sinoatrial node, AV node and myocardium are Gs-coupled, raising cAMP when stimulated by noradrenaline or adrenaline
The blocker competitively antagonises these receptors, reducing sympathetic drive: heart rate (negative chronotropy) and contractility (negative inotropy) fall
Cardiac output falls, and MAP is approximately CO x SVR so blood pressure falls
Blockade of renal juxtaglomerular beta-1 receptors reduces renin, angiotensin II and aldosterone
Selectivity for beta-1 spares beta-2 receptors, reducing bronchial and peripheral vascular side effects
questions.explanation: Competitive antagonism removes sympathetic stimulation of the Gs-cAMP pathway in the heart, so the rate and force of contraction fall. The reduced renin release adds to the blood pressure lowering.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman with a long history of asthma is newly diagnosed with hypertension. Which statement about beta-blocker use is most accurate?

options.text: Non-selective beta-blockers such as propranolol are generally avoided because beta-2 blockade can cause bronchospasm
Propranolol is the safest choice because it also treats tremor
All beta-blockers are equally safe in asthma
Beta-blockers dilate the airways in asthma

questions.correctOptionText: Non-selective beta-blockers such as propranolol are generally avoided because beta-2 blockade can cause bronchospasm

distractorRationale.a: Correct: blocking bronchial beta-2 receptors removes sympathetic bronchodilation and can precipitate severe attacks.
distractorRationale.b: Incorrect: tremor control is irrelevant to the risk of bronchospasm.
distractorRationale.c: Incorrect: cardioselective agents are less risky but non-selective agents are contraindicated.
distractorRationale.d: Incorrect: beta-blockers can constrict airways, not dilate them.

questions.explanation: Bronchial smooth muscle expresses beta-2 receptors that keep airways open under sympathetic tone. Non-selective blockers antagonise these receptors, so propranolol and similar drugs can trigger bronchospasm in people with asthma. Alternative antihypertensive classes would normally be chosen.

questions.stem: Describe the cautions that apply when considering a beta-blocker in a patient with asthma, including why a cardioselective agent does not remove the risk completely.
markingGuide: Non-selective beta-blockers block bronchial beta-2 receptors, causing bronchoconstriction that can be severe or fatal
Non-selective agents are generally contraindicated in asthma
Cardioselective agents (e.g. bisoprolol, atenolol) are preferred if a beta-blocker is essential, but selectivity is relative and lost at higher doses
Use only with specialist advice, low starting dose and monitoring (peak flow, symptoms); avoid in acute or poorly controlled asthma
Topical beta-blocker eye drops can be absorbed systemically and cause bronchospasm
Beta-blockers can also reduce the response to beta-2 agonist reliever therapy
questions.explanation: The risk stems from loss of beta-2 mediated bronchodilation. Cardioselective drugs reduce the risk because they bind beta-1 receptors at lower concentrations but, because selectivity is only relative, risk persists especially at higher doses.

questions.stem: True or false: a cardioselective (beta-1 selective) beta-blocker is completely free of effects on beta-2 receptors at all doses.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Cardioselectivity is relative and dose-dependent. At higher doses beta-1 selective blockers also occupy beta-2 receptors, so they can still cause bronchospasm in susceptible patients.

questions.stem: Clonidine lowers blood pressure partly by stimulating alpha-2 receptors in the brainstem. Which is the best explanation of this effect?

options.text: Alpha-2 receptors are Gi-coupled and reduce sympathetic outflow and noradrenaline release
Alpha-2 receptors are Gs-coupled and raise cAMP in the heart
Alpha-2 stimulation causes vasoconstriction in skeletal muscle
Alpha-2 receptors block the release of renin from the kidney only

questions.correctOptionText: Alpha-2 receptors are Gi-coupled and reduce sympathetic outflow and noradrenaline release

distractorRationale.a: Correct: alpha-2 is a Gi-coupled inhibitory receptor; central and presynaptic stimulation lowers sympathetic tone.
distractorRationale.b: Incorrect: Gs coupling is the beta-receptor pathway.
distractorRationale.c: Incorrect: the vasoconstrictor receptor is mainly alpha-1; central alpha-2 effects reduce tone.
distractorRationale.d: Incorrect: the effect is on sympathetic outflow, not selectively renal renin release.

questions.explanation: Alpha-2 receptors couple to Gi, lowering cAMP and reducing transmitter release. In the brainstem and at sympathetic nerve endings this reduces sympathetic outflow and hence blood pressure, a mechanism distinct from beta-blockade.
